data.title: Istebné – Hrádok, a Hallstatt hillfort above the Orava
data.excerpt: Hallstatt people living in the lower Orava valley built a fortified settlement on a rocky promontory above the river Orava, protecting its most vulnerable northern side with a rampart 8 to 10 m high. Excavation uncovered a log palisade with a tower and weaving areas beneath its roof – and three human skeletons buried under the debris of the destroyed defences.
data.metaTitle: Istebné – Hrádok, a Hallstatt hillfort above the Orava
data.metaDescription: A Hallstatt fortified settlement on a rocky promontory above the river Orava, violently captured and later reoccupied in the Early La Tène period.

children.text: Hallstatt people also lived in the area of the lower Orava, on the route of the prehistoric road running up the Orava from Žaškov and Komjatná. In an effort to withstand danger from outside, they built a fortified settlement at Istebné-Hrádok. For this they made use of a rocky promontory above the river Orava, which on the north-west was connected with the rest of the rising ground, today separated from the hillfort by a new road. The area of the hillfort was approximately 0.5 ha. The hillfort lay only some 20–30 m above the surface of the river, sloping to the south. The most vulnerable point was the northern part, and a rampart approximately 8 to 10 m high was therefore built here to protect the hillfort against attack. Beyond the road a brickworks with its clay pit was established in the last century (now a sports ground), and the road itself is a work of modern times. Originally the road did not run in this direction but led from Žaškov along the left bank of the river, upstream along the Orava to Veličná across a ford. To reach Hrádok at Istebné it was necessary to cross the ford at another place or to use a link road from Veličná. The settlement on Hrádok used the river Orava as a natural obstacle.

children.text: The hillfort was seriously damaged in 1898 during the construction of the Orava railway. The south-eastern part of the promontory was cut through by the railway and the banks were sloped off, so that only an insignificant part remained on the southern side and a somewhat larger part on the northern side of the site. The entrance – the gateway – was also destroyed, along with a large part of the settlement on the eastern side, most of the rampart fortification, of the settlement features and so on. A rich hoard of bronze ornaments and diadems was found in one of the huts.

Excavation took place here as early as the 1950s, when a bronze cruciform pin and a ring of doubled bronze wire with tapered ends were found. The remains of the fortification were also uncovered. Further excavation in the area of the rampart bank revealed burnt river gravel almost in the crown of the rampart, where at a depth of 40 cm there was a layer of broken and river stones laid across one another and thus interlocked.

On the eastern side of the hillfort a rampart sloping gently to the south was investigated. At its foot part of a working feature was uncovered. Sherds of a vase-shaped vessel and 13 clay loom weights together with an iron axe were found. The weights were conical, with a hole through them. They were made of clay mixed with chaff, and on one of them clear impressions of a plaited mat were also found. The axe had a socket formed while hot by bending two lobes over one another. A thin band-shaped bracelet and a storage vessel were also found.
 
Excavation continued in the 1960s as well, when Hallstatt sherds and an iron spearhead were found at the hillfort. Medieval sherds also came to light. The defensive rampart was probably remodelled even after its destruction, and so later alterations, as at other sites, here too partly disturbed the original Hallstatt, or Hallstatt–La Tène, situation on the ground. The rampart had foundations heaped up of yellow clay and was strengthened on the north by stone masonry with banks, and on the settlement side by a vertical wall of roundwood. In the body of the rampart there were sandstone blocks and on them a layer of daub and clay burnt red. Among the interesting finds is the impression of a human heel, pressed in while clay was being packed into the joints of the log construction. In the upper layers of the rampart cut there were larger pieces of layered clay daub which may have come from a roof. It therefore seems that the raw clay on the roof was patched up in places where it had been washed out or had cracked. The remains of a watchtower and its log construction were also uncovered.

From the overall situation established, the original state in the crown of the rampart can be reconstructed at least approximately. From the earlier phase a stone wall has survived in its original position, while for the later phase the stone wall was built anew. This stone masonry in the eastern section indicates the sequence of the building work. First of all the main body of the rampart was built, held on the southern side by shuttering of roundwood with tie-beams running into the rampart, and on the north by stone masonry heaped up from the outside with varied fill material.

The palisade of the later phase had a lean-to roof sloping towards the settlement. The interior of the palisade resembled a corridor with daubed walls, faced on the outside with stone masonry and fitted with loopholes giving a view of the surroundings. The corridor, rising gently as far as the northern corner, was crowned at the highest point of the settlement probably by a rectangular tower. This is suggested by the stone footings of its base, which were laid flat in a row. They lay beneath clay daub fallen from the walls, but did not form compact stone masonry. The carbonised remains of wood found between them and the clay daub came from oak and fir. From this highest part the defensive rampart with its palisade turned at an obtuse angle towards the south-east.

children.text: The state of the hillfort before the catastrophe may have been interesting, since a planned layout of huts and ancillary buildings for the inhabitants and for leading persons alike can be assumed here. The violent capture of the hillfort can be traced in its destruction layer, which also covered the skeletons of its former inhabitants. As many as 3 such skeletons were discovered, buried under levelling debris from the destroyed palisade and the collapsed rampart.

The defensive earthen rampart, rising towards the north-east, may have had a bank considerably higher than it is today, following the outer ground level with the same difference in height. The stones laid in its body formed a stabilising core and helped in the construction of the rampart body. The log palisade built in the crown of the rampart reached a width of 8 m, and 5.5 m at the highest point. The timber construction of the tower was probably daubed with clay on the inside, which after the destruction formed the thickest layer of fired clay, slumped and uncovered on the settlement side. In this space along the log shuttering of the earthen rampart there were originally working areas under a roof for weaving cloth. For this purpose the high log wall was evidently used to hang the warp with clay weights.

In the levelling layer and in the hollows of the rampart there already occurred sherds with applied knobs and crescents, and even La Tène combed pottery. From fragments of an amphora with fine grooving and an applied crescent we recognise that at Istebné-Hrádok the Hallstatt settlement survived into the Early La Tène period, when applied elements appear on Hallstatt material – elements that dominate in the La Tène period and characterise the decoration of Púchov culture pottery. Istebné-Hrádok was indeed still occupied in the La Tène period after the destruction, but it was left abandoned by the end of the La Tène and the Early Roman period. Two iron sickles may come from the last occupation. These agricultural tools point to a hamlet which may have been situated at the foot of Hrádok, close to cultivated fields, as at Sedliacka Dubová.

Already in the Hallstatt period every fortified settlement had its own economic hinterland. Istebné-Hrádok may have had a farming hamlet in the valley of the Istebniansky stream and it also partly shared in the territory of the Veličná Basin.
